title: Mind and brain
content_html:
Mind and brain

Physical brain

The brain is a tangible, biological organ made of neurons, glia, synapses, and circuits. Material, measurable, observable. Its processes include electrochemical signalling, oscillations, plasticity, synaptic changes. It encodes and stores traces (hippocampus binding, cortical distribution) and uses networks and neurotransmitters to consolidate and retrieve. For example, Hippocampal neurons firing together during recall of a childhood scene.

Although we talk about “areas” (hippocampus, amygdala, cortex, etc.), they are nodes in a network, not isolated boxes. The brain’s power comes from connectivity: white-matter tracts, long-range projections, and synchronised rhythms. Bbundles of myelinated axons connecting regions, bridges between left and right hemispheres, links frontal, parietal, and hippocampal areas, chemical signalling (e.g., dopamine for reward, acetylcholine for attention) tunes networks across areas. Oscillatory synchrony (brain rhythms) temporally align activity in distant regions - like an internal Wi-Fi.

Neuroscience describes networks rather than locations: The Default Mode Network descibes episodic memory, self-projection, imagination. The Salience Network detects important stimuli, toggles attention. A Central Executive Network controls working memory, planning, decision-making. These networks are built from distributed hubs connected by tracts and synchronised rhythms.

Segmentation ensures specialisation (vision in occipital cortex, emotion in amygdala), connectivity ensures integration (seeing a face + feeling trust + recalling a name) so that reconstruction of memory is only possible because these segments re-communicate and re-synchronise at recall. The brain is not a collection of separate storage boxes, it is a segmented, specialised system wired into dynamic networks, communicating through axonal tracts, relay hubs, neurotransmitters, and synchronised rhythms.

Memory, perception, and action all depend on this integration.

Mind

The mind is an emergent phenomenon, a subjective experience of thoughts, feelings, awareness, and memory. It arises from brain activity but is not reducible to physical parts alone. Consciousness, intentionality, interpretation, meaning-making… it constructs the “story” or narrative of experience, and imbues raw data with significance (emotion, identity, context). For example, the feeling of nostalgia, meaning, and self-continuity when recalling that same childhood scene.

The brain provides the substrate; the mind emerges from dynamic interactions of neural processes. Memory illustrates this duality: Brain side: distributed traces, synaptic weights, replay mechanisms; Mind side: recollection as a lived moment, reshaped by meaning and awareness.

Brain explains the mechanisms (neurons, circuits, plasticity), mind explains the experience (recollection, meaning, consciousness). Both levels are needed: neuroscience without phenomenology misses the lived dimension; phenomenology without neuroscience lacks mechanism.

Totality of Mind

In Buddhism, the totality of mind (and therefore memory) cannot be fully explained by the physical brain - because mind is understood as an interdependent, luminous continuum that transcends neural processes. Neuroscience, by contrast, ties memory to the brain’s physical architecture. In many Buddhist traditions, mind (citta) is not reducible to the physical body or brain. The brain is seen as a basis or condition, but not the full explanation of consciousness and memory. Consciousness (vijñāna) is described as one of the five aggregates (skandhas) - form, sensation, perception, formations, and consciousness - which arise dependently (pratītyasamutpāda). In Yogācāra (“Mind-Only”) schools, memory is tied to the ālayavijñāna (“storehouse consciousness”), which preserves karmic seeds (bīja) across lifetimes. This implies continuity beyond the physical brain. In Mahāyāna, ultimate mind is often described as luminous, empty, non-local, not constrained by physical architecture. From a Buddhist point of view, memory is not fully contained within neural tissue, it also reflects karmic imprints and a continuum of consciousness that transcends one lifetime.

Modern neuroscience explains memory in terms of neural networks, synaptic plasticity, and engrams. This model is powerful for understanding encoding, storage, and retrieval during life, but it doesn’t address continuity across death or rebirth. Neuroscience tends to treat consciousness as an emergent property of brain activity, not something that persists independently. Some modern Buddhist thinkers and neuroscientists (e.g., Francisco Varela, the Dalai Lama’s dialogues with cognitive scientists) explore whether subjective experience can be accounted for by physicalist models, or whether something is left out.

Mind and memory

Mind and memory are co-defining. To have a mind (in the functional, experiential sense) is to process, retain, and recall information over time. Without memory, there is no continuity of consciousness - only isolated moments. Thus, ==memory is not an add-on but a constitutive element of mind itself.==

The brain’s physical architecture - neurons, synapses, circuits - is the substrate where both mind and memory arise. Neural activity (thoughts, perceptions) and synaptic change (memory traces) are two aspects of the same underlying processes. Empirical evidence (e.g., amnesia from hippocampal damage, memory modulation via optogenetics) shows that altering brain structure/function directly alters memory and therefore the continuity of mind. So on the one hand, mind and memory are inseparable from the physical brain - they emerge from its dynamics and plasticity. On the other hand, mind and memory cannot be reduced only to physical processes - they are inseparable in experience, but may extend beyond the brain (e.g., karmic continuity, ālayavijñāna).
